chapters.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces Newton's three laws of motion as central principles of classical physics. It covers the relationships between force, mass, and acceleration, and discusses how these laws can be applied to analyze the motion of particles and systems. The chapter also addresses frames of reference and the foundational definitions needed to work with these laws.
key_concepts: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)
Newton's Second Law of Motion (F = ma)

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook covers classical mechanics with a focus on Newton's Laws of Motion. It explores the foundational principles of force, mass, and acceleration that underpin classical physics. The material is presented to make the laws straightforward to apply in a variety of physical scenarios.

events.text: If net force = 0, then acceleration = 0. Object stays still or moves at constant velocity in a straight line.
Inertial frame: a reference frame in which Newton's First Law holds correctly.
Non-inertial frame: an accelerating frame where the First Law appears to break down.
Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is itself inertial.
Bigger force → bigger acceleration. Bigger mass → smaller acceleration (for same force).
F_net is the vector sum of ALL forces acting on the object.
Acceleration exists at the same instant as the net force — no delay.
Step 1: Choose your system — every part must share the same acceleration (same size and direction).
Step 2: List every force acting on the system from outside. Ignore internal forces.
Step 3: Draw a free body diagram — represent the system as a dot, draw and label every external force as an arrow.
Step 4: Choose axes (x along acceleration direction), then write F_net = ma for each axis.
Always: choose system → list external forces → draw free body diagram → apply F=ma along each axis.
If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. Always.
Third Law pairs ALWAYS act on different objects — never on the same object.
Tension = magnitude of the mutual pull between two halves of a string at any cross-section.
Massless string → tension is uniform throughout. Massive string → tension varies along its length.

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_1>>
Welcome to Chapter 5 — Newton's Laws of Motion. Over the next several topics, we are going to build up one of the most powerful frameworks in all of physics, starting right now with the First Law. <<SECTION:Newton's First Law of Motion|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_1:force_balance>> Take a look at the board here. You can see three situations — a book on a table, a hockey puck sliding on ice, and a ball hanging from a string. What do they all have in common? In each case, we can say something precise about the forces acting on the object. And that precision is exactly what Newton's First Law gives us. <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the statement: if the total force acting on an object is zero, the object will not accelerate. <<WRITE_KEY:If net force = 0, then acceleration = 0. Object stays still or moves at constant velocity in a straight line.|id=key-1>> That means it either stays perfectly still, or it keeps moving at a constant speed in a straight line — forever, unless something changes. And it works the other way too. If you observe that an object is not accelerating, you can be absolutely certain the forces on it are balanced and add up to zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Think about that book on the board. Gravity pulls it downward. The table pushes it upward. The book is not accelerating, so those two forces must be perfectly equal and opposite. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{	ext{gravity}} + F_{	ext{normal}} = 0|id=eq-1>> If you yanked the table away, the upward force vanishes, the forces are no longer balanced, and the book accelerates downward. The law predicted that the moment you changed the forces. <<PAUSE:long>> Now here is where things get really interesting, and this is a subtlety that a lot of people miss. The law only works if you are measuring from the right kind of reference frame. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_1:inertial_frames>> Look at this comparison on the board. On the left, a train moving at perfectly constant velocity. On the right, a train that is speeding up. Imagine a lamp hanging inside an elevator whose cable has just snapped. Someone standing on the ground watches the lamp fall — they correctly say the forces are not balanced. But someone sitting inside the falling elevator sees the lamp just hanging there, perfectly still. They might wrongly conclude the forces are balanced. Both cannot be right at the same time. <<PAUSE:short>> This leads us to a crucial definition. <<WRITE_TEXT:Inertial frame: a reference frame in which Newton's First Law holds correctly.|id=text-1>> A frame where the law works correctly is called an inertial frame. A frame where it breaks down — like the inside of that falling elevator — is called a non-inertial frame. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-inertial frame: an accelerating frame where the First Law appears to break down.|id=text-2>> The Earth itself is not a perfect inertial frame because it rotates and moves, but for everyday problems it is close enough that we treat it as one. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is a beautiful bonus result. Any frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame. <<WRITE_KEY:Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is itself inertial.|id=key-2>> That steady train on the left of the diagram — physics inside it obeys the First Law just as well as it does on the ground. The moment the train speeds up or slows down, you are in a non-inertial frame, and the law no longer applies directly. <<PAUSE:long>> Now that we have the First Law firmly in hand, the natural next question is: what happens when the forces are not balanced? How exactly does an object respond? That is precisely what Newton's Second Law answers, and we will dig into it right now.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_2>>
Now that we have seen how Newton's First Law describes what happens when forces are balanced, let's move on to the Second Law — which tells us exactly what happens when they are not. <<SECTION:Newton's Second Law of Motion|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_2:f_ma_core>> Look at the board here. You can see the core relationship laid out visually — force, mass, and acceleration, and how they connect to each other. Here is the big idea: the acceleration of an object equals the total force acting on it divided by its mass. In other words, force equals mass times acceleration. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{F}_{	ext{net}} = m\vec{a}|id=eq-1>> That is the heart of it. Let me unpack why this is so powerful. <<PAUSE:short>> Acceleration is how quickly something speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. Force is the push or pull causing that change. And mass is basically how much stuff is in the object — how hard it is to get moving or to stop. So if you push something with a bigger force, you get a bigger acceleration. And if the object has a bigger mass, the same force gives you a smaller acceleration. <<WRITE_TEXT:Bigger force → bigger acceleration. Bigger mass → smaller acceleration (for same force).|id=text-1>> Think about pushing a shopping cart versus pushing a car with the same effort. The car barely moves because its mass is so much greater. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, one really important detail. We are talking about the total force — the vector sum of all forces acting on the particle at once. <<WRITE_TEXT:F_net is the vector sum of ALL forces acting on the object.|id=text-2>> If someone pushes a box to the right and friction pushes it to the left, you must add those forces together, taking direction into account, before you can figure out the acceleration. <<PAUSE:long>> Here is another subtlety worth pausing on. The law says the acceleration happens at the exact same instant as the force. <<WRITE_KEY:Acceleration exists at the same instant as the net force — no delay.|id=key-1>> The moment you stop pushing, the acceleration drops to zero right then and there. Not a moment later. There is no delay. <<PAUSE:short>> Think about a rocket launching into space. The engines produce a massive force. Force divided by the rocket's mass gives it a tremendous upward acceleration. As the rocket burns fuel and gets lighter, the same engine force now acts on a smaller mass — so the acceleration actually increases as the rocket climbs. That is the Second Law working in real time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a =  rac{F_{	ext{net}}}{m}|id=eq-2>> <<PAUSE:long>> And remember — all of this is measured from an inertial frame, just as we established with the First Law. The Second Law and the First Law are deeply connected. The First Law is actually a special case of the Second — when the net force is zero, the acceleration is zero, which is exactly what the First Law says. <<PAUSE:short>> We now have a precise mathematical tool for predicting motion. But knowing the law and actually applying it to real problems are two different things. In the next topic, we will build a careful, step-by-step method for doing exactly that.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3>>
Now that we have the Second Law in hand, let's talk about how to actually use it. Knowing that force equals mass times acceleration is one thing — applying it correctly to a real problem is another skill entirely. Think of it like a recipe. If you skip steps or rush, you end up with the wrong answer. So let me walk you through a careful, four-step process that works for almost every mechanics problem you will ever meet. <<SECTION:Applying Newton's Laws — Four-Step Method|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3:four_step_process>> Look at the flowchart on the board. Four steps, in order. Let's go through each one. <<PAUSE:short>> Step one: choose your system. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Choose your system — every part must share the same acceleration (same size and direction).|id=step-1>> This is the most important decision you make. The rule is that every part of your chosen system must have exactly the same acceleration — same size, same direction. If a block sits on top of another block and they slide together, treat them as one system. But if one part moves up while another moves sideways, their accelerations point in different directions, and you cannot lump them together. <<PAUSE:short>> Step two: list every external force. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 2: List every force acting on the system from outside. Ignore internal forces.|id=step-2>> Only forces that other things exert on your system belong on this list. Forces your system exerts on other things do not. This is where students often get confused, so be really careful. <<PAUSE:short>> Step three: draw a free body diagram. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 3: Draw a free body diagram — represent the system as a dot, draw and label every external force as an arrow.|id=step-3>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3:free_body_diagram_examples>> Look at these side-by-side examples on the board. The same physical situation — a boy balancing a bag on his head — produces completely different force lists depending on whether you choose the boy or the bag as your system. That is why step one comes first. Your free body diagram is your map. Without it, you are navigating in the dark. <<PAUSE:long>> Step four: choose your axes and apply the Second Law. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 4: Choose axes (x along acceleration direction), then write F_net = ma for each axis.|id=step-4>> A great tip is to point your x-axis in the direction the object is actually accelerating. Then write out the Second Law separately for each axis. Along the direction of acceleration, forces add up to mass times acceleration. Along the perpendicular direction, if there is no acceleration, forces balance and add up to zero. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3:angled_tension_example>> Look at this example on the board — a block pulled by a string angled upward. The block accelerates horizontally to the right, so we point the x-axis that way. The tension has a horizontal component — tension times cosine of the angle — and that is what drives the acceleration. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T\cos	heta = ma|id=eq-1>> Along the vertical axis, there is no acceleration, so the normal force plus the vertical component of tension must balance gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:N + T\sin	heta - mg = 0|id=eq-2>> Notice that the normal force is less than the full weight of the block, because the string is helping to support some of it. Choosing your axes wisely makes the math clean and the physics clear. <<WRITE_KEY:Always: choose system → list external forces → draw free body diagram → apply F=ma along each axis.|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> This four-step method is the backbone of everything we will do in mechanics. In the next topic, we will add one more powerful tool to our kit — Newton's Third Law — which tells us something profound about how forces always come in pairs.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_4>>
Now that we have a solid method for applying Newton's laws, let's add one more fundamental law to our toolkit — Newton's Third Law. And I want to warn you upfront: this is one of the most elegant ideas in physics, and also one of the most misunderstood. <<SECTION:Newton's Third Law of Motion|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_4:action_reaction_pairs>> Look at the board. Two classic scenarios — a person pushing a wall, and a block sitting on a table. In each case, you can see the force pairs highlighted. Here is the core idea: forces always come in pairs. <<WRITE_KEY:If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. Always.|id=key-1>> If object A pushes or pulls on object B, then object B pushes or pulls back on object A with exactly the same strength but in the opposite direction. Always. No exceptions. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is the crucial thing that trips people up. These two paired forces act on different objects. They never act on the same object. <<WRITE_TEXT:Third Law pairs ALWAYS act on different objects — never on the same object.|id=text-1>> So when you are figuring out the motion of one particular object, you only write down the force that acts on that object — not its partner. The table pushes the block upward. The block pushes the table downward. When we study the block's motion, we only care about the upward push on the block. The downward push on the table is irrelevant to the block's equation of motion. <<PAUSE:long>> Now let's talk about tension in a string, which is a beautiful application of the Third Law. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_4:tension_in_strings>> Look at the diagram on the board. Imagine slicing a string at any point. The two halves pull on each other at that cut — the lower half pulls the upper half down, and the upper half pulls the lower half up, with equal force. That common magnitude is what we call tension. <<WRITE_TEXT:Tension = magnitude of the mutual pull between two halves of a string at any cross-section.|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is a really useful shortcut. If a string has no mass at all — a massless string — the tension is exactly the same at every point along it. <<WRITE_key:Massless string → tension is uniform throughout. Massive string → tension varies along its length.|id=key-2>> But if the string has mass, the tension changes from one end to the other, because the string itself has weight that needs to be supported. Look at the diagram — you can see how the tension at the top of a massive string is greater than at the bottom, because the top must support both the hanging object and the weight of the string below it. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T_{	ext{top}} = T_{	ext{bottom}} + m_{	ext{string}} \cdot g|id=eq-1>> When a string passes over a light, frictionless pulley, the tension is the same on both sides of that pulley too. These are powerful shortcuts for solving problems quickly and correctly. <<PAUSE:long>> In the next topic, we are going to encounter a situation where Newton's laws seem to break down — when you are inside an accelerating frame of reference. We will see how to handle that with a clever trick called pseudo forces.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_5>>
Now that we have all three of Newton's laws in hand, let's tackle something really interesting — what happens when you try to use those laws from inside an accelerating vehicle or any other accelerating frame of reference. <<SECTION:Pseudo Forces in Non-Inertial Frames|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_5:inertial_vs_noninertial>> Look at the board. On the left, a pendulum in a car as seen from the ground — an inertial frame. On the right, the same pendulum as seen from inside the accelerating car — a non-inertial frame. Notice how the description of what is happening looks completely different depending on where you are standing. <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the core issue. When we measure the motion of an object from inside an accelerating frame, we get a different acceleration than someone standing still on the road would measure. The two accelerations differ by exactly the acceleration of the frame itself. When we write Newton's Second Law from inside the accelerating frame, an extra term appears. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{F}_{	ext{net}} + \vec{F}_{	ext{pseudo}} = m\vec{a}_{	ext{frame}}|id=eq-1>> That extra term is the mass of the object multiplied by the acceleration of the frame, and it points in the opposite direction to the frame's acceleration. <<WRITE_KEY:Pseudo force = −m × (acceleration of the frame). Points opposite to the frame's acceleration.|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now, we are so used to Newton's laws that we would love to keep using them even in these tricky situations. So here is the clever trick: we pretend that extra term is an actual force. We call it a pseudo force, or sometimes an inertial force. It is not a real force — no object is actually pushing on you — but if we include it in our list of forces and then apply Newton's Second Law as usual, we get the right answer. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pseudo force is not real — no object exerts it. It is a bookkeeping tool for non-inertial frames.|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_5:pseudo_force_examples>> Look at these three scenarios on the board — an elevator accelerating upward, a train accelerating forward, and a rotating carnival ride. In each case, you can see the real forces and the pseudo force side by side. Let me walk through the pendulum example in detail. The car accelerates forward with some acceleration. From inside the car, the pendulum bob hangs at an angle and appears to be in equilibrium. To explain that equilibrium using Newton's Second Law, we include a pseudo force pointing backward — opposite to the car's acceleration. <<WRITE_EQUATION:	an	heta =  rac{a_{	ext{frame}}}{g}|id=eq-2>> The string tension, gravity, and the pseudo force all balance, and that equation tells us the angle the string makes with the vertical. <<PAUSE:short>> Think about an elevator accelerating upward. From inside, you feel heavier. We add a pseudo force pointing downward, equal to your mass times the elevator's acceleration. This pseudo force adds to gravity, making the floor push up on you harder than usual. <<WRITE_EQUATION:N = m(g + a_{	ext{elevator}})|id=eq-3>> No new real force appeared — it is just the effect of being in an accelerating frame, captured neatly by the pseudo force idea. <<PAUSE:long>> The key thing to remember is this: pseudo forces only appear when you are working from a non-inertial frame. Step outside and watch from the ground, and you do not need them at all. Now, this idea of non-inertial frames and pseudo forces actually sets up a beautiful puzzle that we will look at next — the famous horse and cart problem.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_6>>
Now let's look at one of the most classic puzzles in all of physics — the horse and cart problem. It trips up a lot of people the first time they hear it, and working through it carefully will sharpen everything we have learned so far about Newton's laws. <<SECTION:The Horse and Cart Problem|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_6:horse_cart_forces>> Look at the force diagram on the board. You can see the horse, the cart, and every force on each object clearly separated. Here is the puzzle. A horse pulls a cart forward. By Newton's Third Law, the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. So the two forces cancel out, and nothing should move — right? <<PAUSE:short>> Wrong. And figuring out exactly why is the whole point. <<WRITE_KEY:Newton's Third Law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects. Never add them together when analyzing one object's motion.|id=key-1>> The mistake is a sneaky one. We are mixing up forces that act on different objects. Newton's Third Law pairs are always between two objects, but when we want to find out how something accelerates, we only look at the forces acting on that one thing. <<PAUSE:short>> So let us be careful and choose our system. If we pick just the cart, the only force we care about is the force the horse exerts on the cart in the forward direction. <<WRITE_STEP:Choose the cart as system → only force is the horse pulling it forward → cart accelerates forward.|id=step-1>> The force the cart pulls back on the horse? That does not belong in the cart's equation at all. <<PAUSE:long>> Now let us think about the horse. The cart does pull the horse backward, so why does the horse move forward? Because we forgot something important — the ground. <<WRITE_STEP:For the horse: ground pushes horse forward (friction). Cart pulls horse backward. Net force forward → horse accelerates forward.|id=step-2>> When the horse pushes its hooves backward against the road, the road pushes the horse forward. This is friction from the ground, and it has a forward component. If that forward push from the ground is bigger than the backward pull from the cart, the horse accelerates forward. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{	ext{ground on horse}} - F_{	ext{cart on horse}} = m_{	ext{horse}} \cdot a|id=eq-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Similarly, the road pushes back slightly on the cart's wheels, which slightly reduces the cart's acceleration. But the beautiful result is that these friction forces automatically adjust so that the horse and cart end up with the same acceleration and move together as one unit. <<WRITE_TEXT:The horse and cart reach the same acceleration because friction forces self-adjust.|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> The big lesson here is this: always decide what your system is, then list every single force acting on that system and nothing else. Leave out forces that act on other objects. Never leave out forces that act on your system. Only then can you correctly apply the rule that net force equals mass times acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>> This problem is a perfect capstone for everything we have covered so far. In the next topic, we will zoom out and talk about the underlying property that makes all of Newton's laws tick — inertia.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_7>>
We have now worked through all three of Newton's laws and seen how to apply them. But let's take a step back and talk about the underlying property that makes all of this tick — inertia. You already know from Newton's First Law that an object at rest tends to stay at rest, and an object moving in a straight line at constant speed tends to keep doing exactly that. Inertia is just the name we give to that tendency. <<SECTION:Inertia and Mass|id=section-1>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_7:inertia_comparison>> Look at the board. On the left, a tennis ball. On the right, a bowling ball. The same force is applied to each. The tennis ball shoots off quickly. The bowling ball barely moves. Both felt the same force, yet their accelerations were very different. The bowling ball resisted the change in its motion far more. That resistance is inertia. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is the key connection. The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has. Mass and inertia are two sides of the same coin. <<WRITE_KEY:Inertia is the resistance of an object to changes in its state of motion. More mass = more inertia.|id=key-1>> A large mass means a large resistance to acceleration. A small mass means the object is easier to get moving or to stop. <<PAUSE:short>> The mathematical heart of this idea comes straight from Newton's Second Law. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a =  rac{F}{m}|id=eq-1>> For the same force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration. Inertia is not a force itself — it is a property, a measure of how much an object fights back against being accelerated. <<WRITE_TEXT:Inertia is a property of matter, not a force. It is measured by mass.|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_7:newton_first_law>> Look at this diagram on the board. Two scenarios — an object at rest staying at rest, and an object in motion continuing in a straight line. Both are demonstrations of inertia. In everyday life, friction always slows things down, which is why it can feel like objects naturally stop. But that stopping is caused by a force — friction — not by some natural tendency to come to rest. Without friction, a moving object would keep going forever. That is inertia. <<PAUSE:short>> Think about a passenger in a car that suddenly brakes hard. The car slows down rapidly because the brakes apply a large force to it. But the passenger's body keeps wanting to move forward at the original speed. The passenger's mass resists the sudden change in velocity. The seatbelt has to step in and apply a force to slow the passenger down along with the car. Without that force, the passenger would just keep going forward. <<WRITE_TEXT:Seatbelt example: without a force, the passenger's inertia keeps them moving forward when the car brakes.|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:long>> And here is a classic demonstration of inertia in its purest form. Place a coin on a piece of cardboard resting on a glass. Flick the cardboard away sharply. The coin drops straight into the glass rather than flying off with the cardboard. The coin was at rest, and the very brief flick did not apply enough force for long enough to drag the coin along. The coin simply stayed where it was, and gravity pulled it down. <<WRITE_KEY:Inertia keeps an object in its current state — at rest or in uniform motion — until a net force acts on it.|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:long>> And that brings us to the end of this chapter on Newton's Laws of Motion. We started with the First Law — the idea that objects resist changes in their motion. We built up to the Second Law — the precise mathematical relationship between force, mass, and acceleration. We explored the Third Law — the beautiful symmetry of force pairs. We learned how to apply these laws systematically, how to handle non-inertial frames with pseudo forces, and how to untangle the horse and cart puzzle. And now we see that inertia — the property of mass — is the thread running through all of it. In the next chapter, we will take these tools and apply them to specific types of forces — friction, tension, and normal forces — in much more complex and realistic situations.

topics.our_understanding:
Newton's First Law of Motion is one of the most powerful ideas in all of physics, and it says something beautifully simple: if the total force acting on an object is zero, then the object will not accelerate. That means it either stays perfectly still or keeps moving at a constant speed in a straight line. And it works the other way too — if you know an object is not accelerating, you can be absolutely sure the forces on it are balanced and add up to zero. Think about that for a moment. It connects what you see happening to what forces must be acting. That is a remarkable tool.

But here is where things get really interesting. The law only works if you are measuring from the right kind of reference frame. Imagine a lamp hanging inside an elevator whose cable has just snapped. Someone standing on the ground watches the lamp fall with an acceleration of about nine point eight metres per second squared. They correctly say the forces on the lamp are not balanced. But someone sitting inside the falling elevator sees the lamp just hanging there, perfectly still. They might wrongly conclude the forces are balanced. Both observers cannot be right at the same time, so at least one of them is using a bad frame of reference to apply the law.

This leads us to a crucial definition. A frame of reference in which Newton's First Law works correctly is called an inertial frame. A frame where it breaks down — like the inside of that falling elevator — is called a non-inertial frame. The earth itself is not a perfect inertial frame because it rotates and moves, but for everyday problems it is close enough that we treat it as one.

Here is a beautiful bonus result: any frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame. If a train rolls along at a perfectly steady speed, the physics inside that train obeys Newton's First Law just as well as it does on the ground. The key word is constant — the moment the train speeds up or slows down, you are in a non-inertial frame and the law no longer applies directly.
examples: Imagine a book sitting on your desk. Gravity pulls it downward, and the table pushes it upward with a contact force. The book is not accelerating, so Newton's First Law tells us those two forces must be perfectly balanced and add up to zero. If you suddenly removed the table, the upward contact force disappears, the forces are no longer balanced, and the book accelerates downward. The law predicted exactly what would happen just by looking at the forces.

Think about a hockey puck sliding across a nearly frictionless ice surface. Once it is moving, almost no net force acts on it, so it keeps gliding at the same speed in the same direction. This is Newton's First Law in action — no net force means no change in motion. In everyday life friction always slows things down, which is why it can feel like objects naturally stop. But that stopping is caused by a force, not by some natural tendency to rest.

Picture yourself on a smoothly sailing cruise ship crossing a calm ocean at a perfectly steady speed. You place a glass of water on a table. The glass just sits there, perfectly still relative to you. The forces on it are balanced. Newton's First Law works perfectly here because the ship is moving at constant velocity — it is an inertial frame. Now imagine the ship suddenly accelerates forward. The glass slides backward on the table even though nothing seems to push it. That is the non-inertial frame effect — the law appears to break down because your frame of reference is now accelerating.

A heavy ball of mass half a kilogram hangs from a string attached to the ceiling of a room. The ball is at rest, so its acceleration is zero. Newton's First Law tells us immediately that the forces must cancel out. Gravity pulls the ball downward with a force of about four point nine newtons, so the string must be pulling it upward with exactly four point nine newtons. We did not need to do any complicated experiment — the law gave us the answer the moment we knew the ball was not moving.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, so Newton's First Law told us that objects keep doing what they're doing unless a force acts on them. Now the Second Law takes things a step further and actually tells us exactly how much an object changes its motion when a force does act on it. Here is the big idea: the acceleration of an object equals the total force acting on it divided by its mass. In words, force equals mass times acceleration. That is the heart of it. Let me unpack why this is so powerful. Acceleration is how quickly something speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. Force is the push or pull causing that change. And mass is basically how much stuff is in the object — how hard it is to get moving or to stop. So if you push something with a bigger force, you get a bigger acceleration. Makes sense, right? And if the object has a bigger mass, the same force gives you a smaller acceleration. Think about pushing a shopping cart versus pushing a car with the same effort — the car barely moves because its mass is so much greater. Now, one really important detail here: we are talking about the total force, meaning the vector sum of all forces acting on the particle at once. If someone is pushing a box to the right and friction is pushing it to the left, you have to add those forces together, taking direction into account, before you can figure out the acceleration. Also notice this: the law says the acceleration happens at the exact same instant as the force. The moment you stop pushing, the acceleration drops to zero right then and there — not a moment later. There is no delay. And all of this is measured from what we call an inertial frame, which is just a reference point that is not itself accelerating. This law is truly a law of nature — it describes how the universe actually behaves, and it works every single time.
examples: Imagine you are kicking a football and a bowling ball with the same strength kick. The football flies far down the field, but the bowling ball barely rolls a few centimetres. Both received the same force, but the bowling ball has much greater mass, so its acceleration is much smaller. This is Newton's Second Law in action — greater mass means less acceleration for the same force.

Think about a rocket launching into space. The engines produce a massive force by burning fuel and pushing hot gases downward. Because force equals mass times acceleration, the huge force divided by the rocket's mass gives it a tremendous upward acceleration. As the rocket burns fuel and gets lighter, the same engine force now acts on a smaller mass, so the acceleration actually increases as the rocket climbs higher.

Picture two identical toy cars on a smooth floor. You flick the first one gently and it rolls slowly. You flick the second one twice as hard and it rolls twice as fast. The mass is the same in both cases, so doubling the force doubles the acceleration. This direct relationship between force and acceleration is exactly what the Second Law predicts.

Here is a subtle but important point: suppose you are pushing a heavy box across the floor and you suddenly let go. The moment your hands leave the box, the pushing force disappears, and so does the acceleration — instantly. The box does not gradually stop accelerating over the next second; the change is immediate. Force and acceleration are always in step with each other at every single moment in time.

Step 1 : Decide the System
The first step is to decide the system on which the
laws of motion are to be applied. The system may be

topics.our_understanding:
Today we are going to talk about a really practical skill — how to actually use Newton's laws to solve real problems. The laws themselves are elegant, but applying them takes a careful, step-by-step approach. Think of it like a recipe. If you skip steps or rush, you end up with the wrong answer, just like a cake that collapses because you forgot the baking powder.

The first thing you must do is decide your system — that is, which object or group of objects are you going to focus on? This sounds simple, but it is actually the most important decision you make. Here is the key rule: every part of your chosen system must have exactly the same acceleration, meaning the same size and the same direction. Imagine a block sitting on top of another block, and they are sliding together across a table. Since they move as one unit, you can treat them as a single system. But if one part moves up while another moves sideways, you cannot lump them together — their accelerations point in different directions, so they cannot be treated as one particle.

Once you have your system, the second step is to list every force acting on it from the outside. Notice that word — outside. Forces that your system exerts on other things do not belong on your list. Only forces that other things exert on your system. This is where students often get confused, so be really careful here.

Next, you draw a free body diagram. You represent your entire system as a single dot, and you draw arrows coming out of that dot for every force on your list. Label each arrow with what it is — gravity, the normal force from the table, the tension in a string, and so on. This diagram is your map. Without it, you are navigating in the dark.

Finally, you choose your axes cleverly. A great tip is to point your x-axis in the direction the object is actually accelerating. Then you write out Newton's second law — the sum of all forces equals mass times acceleration — separately for each axis. Along the direction of acceleration, the forces add up to mass times acceleration. Along the perpendicular direction, if there is no acceleration, the forces must balance and add up to zero. Solve those equations, and you have your answer. This four-step process works for almost every problem you will ever meet in mechanics.
examples: Imagine you have two books stacked on a desk, and you push them both together with one hand. Since both books move together — same speed, same direction, same acceleration — you can treat them as a single system with a combined mass. The only forces you list are your push, gravity pulling the combined stack down, and the desk pushing up. You would not include the force the bottom book exerts on the top book, because that is an internal force between parts of your system, not an outside force acting on it.

Think about a boy standing still while balancing a heavy bag on his head. Before you can list any forces, you must ask: which system am I looking at? If you choose the boy as your system, the forces on him are gravity pulling him down, the floor pushing him up, and the bag pressing down on his head. If instead you choose the bag as your system, the forces are completely different — now it is gravity pulling the bag down and the boy's head pushing the bag up. Same physical situation, two completely different force lists, depending on which system you picked first.

Picture a block being pulled across a smooth table by a string that is angled upward, not perfectly horizontal. The block accelerates horizontally to the right. So we point our x-axis to the right, in the direction of acceleration. The tension in the string has a horizontal part — tension times cosine of the angle — and that horizontal part is what causes the acceleration, so it equals mass times acceleration. The string also pulls the block slightly upward, which means the table does not need to push up with the full weight of the block. The table's normal force ends up being less than the block's weight because the string is helping to support some of it. This is a beautiful example of how choosing your axes wisely makes the math clean and the physics clear.

Consider a yo-yo hanging still on a string. You choose the yo-yo as your system. Two forces act on it from outside: gravity pulling it straight down, and the string pulling it straight up. Since it is not accelerating, these two forces must be perfectly balanced — they add up to zero. You set up your y-axis pointing upward, write that the tension minus the weight equals zero, and immediately get that the tension equals the weight. Simple, clean, and it all flows from following the four steps carefully.

events.text: Step 1: Choose your system — every part must share the same acceleration (same size and direction).
Step 2: List every force acting on the system from outside. Ignore internal forces.
Step 3: Draw a free body diagram — represent the system as a dot, draw and label every external force as an arrow.
Step 4: Choose axes (x along acceleration direction), then write F_net = ma for each axis.
Always: choose system → list external forces → draw free body diagram → apply F=ma along each axis.

Let's go through each one carefully. <<PAUSE:short>> Step one: choose your system. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Choose your system — every part must share the same acceleration (same size and direction).|id=step-1>> This is the most important decision you make. Every part of your chosen system must have exactly the same acceleration — same size, same direction. If two blocks slide together as one unit, treat them as a single system. But if different parts accelerate in different directions, you cannot lump them together. <<PAUSE:short>> Step two: list every external force. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 2: List every force acting on the system from outside. Ignore internal forces.|id=step-2>> Only forces that other objects exert on your system belong here. Forces your system exerts on other things do not. This is where students most often go wrong, so be deliberate. <<PAUSE:short>> Step three: draw a free body diagram. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 3: Draw a free body diagram — represent the system as a dot, draw and label every external force as an arrow.|id=step-3>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3:free_body_diagram_examples>> Look at these side-by-side examples on the board. The same physical situation — a boy balancing a bag on his head — produces completely different force lists depending on whether you choose the boy or the bag as your system. That is why step one comes first. Your free body diagram is your map. Without it, you are navigating in the dark. <<PAUSE:long>> Step four: choose your axes and apply Newton's Second Law. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 4: Choose axes (x along acceleration direction), then write F_net = ma for each axis.|id=step-4>> Point your x-axis in the direction the object is actually accelerating. Then write the Second Law separately for each axis. Along the acceleration direction, forces sum to mass times acceleration. Along the perpendicular direction, if there is no acceleration, forces must balance to zero. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:newtons_laws_of_motion:5_3:angled_tension_example>> Look at this worked example on the board — a block pulled by a string angled upward from the horizontal. The block accelerates to the right, so we point the x-axis that way. The horizontal component of tension drives the acceleration. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T\cos	heta = ma|id=eq-1>> Along the vertical axis, there is no acceleration, so the normal force plus the upward component of tension must balance gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:N + T\sin	heta - mg = 0|id=eq-2>> Notice that the normal force ends up being less than the block's full weight, because the string is helping to support some of it. Choosing your axes wisely makes the math clean and the physics transparent. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me also show you how the system choice matters with a quick example. Think about a boy standing still while balancing a heavy bag on his head. If you choose the boy as your system, the forces on him are gravity, the floor pushing up, and the bag pressing down. If you choose the bag as your system, the forces are completely different — gravity on the bag and the boy's head pushing the bag up. Same physical situation, two completely different force lists. 5.4 NEWTON’S THIRD LAW OF MOTION
Newton’s third law has already been introduced in
chapter  4. “If  a  body  A  exerts  a  force  F

Thus, the force exerted by A on B and that by B
on A are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
This law connects the forces exerted by two bodies on
one another. The forces connected by the third law act
on two different bodies and hence will never appear
together in the list of forces at step 2 of applying
Newton’s first or second law.
For example, suppose a table exerts an upward
force N  on a block placed on it. This force should be
accounted if we consider the block as the system. The
block pushes the table down with an equal force N .
But this force acts on the table and should be
considered only if we take the table as the system.
Thus, only one of the two forces connected by the third
law may appear in the equation of motion depending
on the system chosen. The force exerted by the earth
on a particle of mass M is Mg downward and therefore,
by the particle on the earth is Mg upward. These two
forces will not cancel each other. The downward force
on the particle will cause acceleration of the particle
and that on the earth will cause acceleration (how
large ?) of the earth.
 Newton’s third law of motion is not strictly correct
when interaction between two bodies separated by a
large distance is considered. We come across such
deviations when we study electric and magnetic forces.
Working with the Tension in a String
The idea of tension was qualitatively introduced in
chapter 4. Suppose a block of mass M is hanging
through a string from the ceiling (figure 5.9).
Consider a cross-section of the string at A. The
cross-section divides the string in two parts, lower part
and the upper part. The two parts are in physical
contact at the cross-section at A. The lower part of the
string will exert an electromagnetic force on the upper
part and the upper part will exert an electromagnetic
force on the lower part. According to the third law,
these two forces will have equal magnitude. The lower
part pulls down the upper part with a force T and the
upper part pulls up the lower part with equal force T.
The common magnitude of the forces exerted by the
two parts of the string on each other is called the
tension in the string at A. What is the tension in the
string at the lower end ? The block and the string are
in contact at this end and exert electromagnetic forces
on each other. The common magnitude of these forces
is the tension in the string at the lower end. What is
the tension in the string at the upper end ? At this
end, the string and the ceiling meet. The string pulls
the ceiling down and the ceiling pulls the string up.
The common magnitude of these forces is the tension
in the string at the upper end.

topics.our_understanding:
Newton's Third Law is one of the most elegant ideas in all of physics, and it's also one of the most misunderstood. Here's the core idea: forces always come in pairs. If object A pushes or pulls on object B, then object B pushes or pulls back on object A with exactly the same strength but in the opposite direction. Always. No exceptions in everyday situations. Think about that for a moment — you can never have a lone force in the universe. Every single force has a partner force pointing the other way.

Now here's the crucial thing that trips people up. These two paired forces act on different objects. They never act on the same object. So when you're figuring out the motion of one particular object, you only write down the force that acts on that object — not its partner. For example, a table pushes a block upward with a normal force. The block pushes the table downward with an equal force. But when we study the block's motion, we only care about the upward push on the block. The downward push on the table is irrelevant to the block's equation of motion.

This brings us to tension in a string, which is a beautiful application of the third law. Imagine slicing a string at any point. The two halves pull on each other at that cut — the lower half pulls the upper half down, and the upper half pulls the lower half up, with equal force. That common magnitude of force is what we call tension. Tension is essentially the string's internal tug-of-war at any given point.

Here's a really useful shortcut: if a string has no mass at all — we call it a massless string — then the tension is exactly the same at every single point along the string. But if the string has mass, the tension changes from one end to the other, because the string itself has weight that needs to be supported. When a string passes over a light, frictionless pulley, the tension is the same on both sides of that pulley too. These are powerful tools for solving problems quickly and correctly.
examples: Imagine you're standing on a skateboard and you push against a wall. You push the wall forward, and the wall pushes you backward — that's why you roll away from the wall. The force you exert on the wall and the force the wall exerts on you are a Newton's Third Law pair. They're equal in size, opposite in direction, and they act on different objects — one on the wall, one on you. That's why only the force on you matters when figuring out your acceleration on the skateboard.

Think about a block hanging from a string attached to the ceiling. The Earth pulls the block downward with a gravitational force equal to the block's mass times g. By Newton's Third Law, the block pulls the Earth upward with that exact same force. Now you might wonder — why don't these two forces cancel out? The answer is they act on different objects. The downward force acts on the block and causes the block to accelerate downward if unsupported. The upward force acts on the Earth. The Earth is so incredibly massive that this tiny upward pull causes an acceleration so small we could never measure it.

Now picture a heavy block hanging from a string, and the string itself has some mass too. If you cut the string mentally at a point halfway up, the lower half of the string is being pulled down by both the block's weight and its own weight. The upper half has to support all of that. So the tension at the top of the string is greater than the tension at the bottom. The tension at the very bottom just equals the block's weight, because at that point the string only needs to hold up the block. As you move up the string, more and more of the string's own weight gets added in, so the tension grows.

Here's a practical shortcut worth remembering. Suppose you have a very thin, light piece of thread — so light you can basically ignore its weight entirely. If you hang a one-kilogram mass from it, the tension is the same everywhere along the thread, from top to bottom. This is the massless string assumption, and it simplifies calculations enormously. In most physics problems, unless you're told the string has a specific mass, you treat it as massless and enjoy the fact that tension is uniform throughout.

topics.our_understanding: Alright, let's talk about something really interesting — what happens when you try to use Newton's laws from inside an accelerating vehicle or any other accelerating frame of reference. We call these accelerating frames 'noninertial frames,' and the tricky thing is that Newton's second law, which says force equals mass times acceleration, doesn't quite work the same way inside them. Here's why. Imagine you're sitting in a car that's accelerating forward. You feel pushed back into your seat, right? But from the road's perspective, nothing is actually pushing you backward — the car is just accelerating forward and you have inertia. So what's going on? When we measure the motion of an object from inside an accelerating frame, we get a different acceleration than someone standing still on the road would measure. The two accelerations differ by exactly the acceleration of the frame itself. When we write Newton's second law from inside the accelerating frame, there's an extra term that appears — it's the mass of the object multiplied by the acceleration of the frame, and it points in the opposite direction to the frame's acceleration. Now, we're so used to Newton's laws that we'd love to keep using them even in these tricky situations. So here's the clever trick: we pretend that extra term is an actual force. We call it a pseudo force, or sometimes an inertial force. It's not a real force — no object is actually pushing on you — but if we include it in our list of forces and then apply Newton's second law as usual, we get the right answer. The pseudo force always has a magnitude of mass times the acceleration of the frame, and it always points opposite to the direction the frame is accelerating. Think of it as a bookkeeping trick that lets us keep using familiar tools even when we're in an unfamiliar, accelerating setting. The key thing to remember is this: pseudo forces only appear when you're working from a noninertial frame. If you step outside and watch from the ground, you don't need them at all.
examples: Think about a pendulum hanging from the ceiling of a car that's accelerating forward along a road. If you're standing on the road watching, you'd say the bob swings backward because the car accelerates forward and the bob has inertia. But if you're sitting inside the car, the bob looks like it's just hanging at an angle and staying still. To explain why it's in equilibrium from inside the car, you need to include a pseudo force pointing backward — opposite to the car's acceleration. The string then balances gravity pulling down, tension pulling along the string, and this pseudo force pulling backward. Working through the balance of these three forces tells you the angle the string makes with the vertical is the inverse tangent of the car's acceleration divided by gravitational acceleration.

Imagine you're in an elevator that's accelerating upward. You feel heavier than usual — like someone added extra weight to your body. That feeling is real, but the cause is a pseudo force. From inside the elevator, which is a noninertial frame accelerating upward, we add a pseudo force pointing downward, equal to your mass times the elevator's acceleration. This pseudo force adds to gravity, making the floor push up on you harder than usual, which is exactly why you feel heavier. No new real force appeared — it's just the effect of being in an accelerating frame, captured neatly by the pseudo force idea.

Picture a ball sitting on the smooth floor of a train that suddenly accelerates forward. From the platform, you'd say the ball stays put because nothing pushed it — the train just moved forward under it. But from inside the train, the ball appears to roll backward on its own, with no visible force causing it. If you want to explain this using Newton's second law from inside the train, you must introduce a pseudo force pointing backward on the ball, equal to the ball's mass times the train's acceleration. This imaginary backward force explains the ball's apparent backward motion perfectly, even though no real object is pushing it.

Think about a spinning carnival ride — the kind where you stand against the wall and the floor drops away. You feel pressed against the wall as if something is pushing you outward. That outward push is a pseudo force called the centrifugal force, and it arises because the ride is a rotating, noninertial frame. From outside the ride, a physicist would say you're just being pushed inward by the wall to keep you moving in a circle. But from inside the ride, including the outward pseudo force lets you use Newton's second law comfortably and still get the right answers about how hard the wall pushes on you.

A good example which illustrates the ideas
discussed in this chapter is the motion of a cart pulled
by a horse. Suppose the cart is at rest when the driver
whips the horse. The horse pulls the cart and the cart
accelerates forward. The question posed is as follows.
The horse pulls the cart by a force F1 in the forward
direction. From the third law of motion the cart pulls
the horse by an equal force F2 = F1 in the backward
direction. The sum of these forces is, therefore, zero
(figure 5.15). Why should then the cart accelerate
forward ?
Try to locate the mistake in the argument.
According to our scheme, we should first decide the
system. We can take the horse as the system or the
cart as the system or the cart and the horse taken
together as the system. Suppose you take the cart as
the system. Then the forces on the cart should be listed
and the forces on the horse should not enter the
discussion. The force on the cart is F1 in the forward
direction and the acceleration of the cart is also in the
forward direction. How much is this acceleration ?
Take the mass of the cart to be MC . Is the acceleration
of the cart a = F1 /MC in forward direction ? Think
carefully. We shall return to this question.

horse. This time we have to consider the forces on the
horse. The forward force F1 by the horse acts on the
cart and it should not be taken into account when we
discuss the motion of the horse. The force on the horse
by the cart is F2 in the backward direction. Why does
the horse go in the forward direction when whipped ?

topics.our_understanding: Here is one of the most classic puzzles in all of physics, and it trips up a lot of people the first time they hear it. A horse pulls a cart forward. By Newton's third law, the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal and opposite force. So the two forces cancel out, and nothing should move, right? Wrong — and figuring out why is the whole point of this section. The mistake is a sneaky one: we are mixing up forces that act on different objects. Newton's third law pairs are always between two objects, but when we want to find out how something accelerates, we only look at the forces acting on that one thing. So let us be careful and choose our system. If we pick just the cart as our system, the only force we care about is the force the horse exerts on the cart in the forward direction. That is the force that accelerates the cart. The force the cart pulls back on the horse? That does not belong in the cart's equation at all. Now let us think about the horse. The cart does pull the horse backward, so why does the horse move forward? Because we forgot something important — the ground. When the horse pushes its hooves backward against the road, the road pushes the horse forward. This is friction from the ground, and it has a forward component. If that forward push from the ground is bigger than the backward pull from the cart, the horse accelerates forward. Similarly, the road also pushes back on the cart's wheels a little, which slightly reduces the cart's acceleration. The beautiful result is that these friction forces automatically adjust themselves so that the horse and cart end up with the same acceleration and move together as one unit. The big lesson here is this: always decide what your system is, then list every single force acting on that system and nothing else. Leave out forces that act on other objects, and never leave out forces that act on your system. Only then can you correctly apply the rule that net force equals mass times acceleration.
examples: Imagine you and a friend are on ice skates, facing each other. You push your friend forward, and by Newton's third law, your friend pushes you backward with the same force. Now, if someone asks why you slide backward, you only think about the forces on you — the push your friend gave you. You do not add in the push you gave your friend, because that force acts on your friend, not on you. This is exactly the same logic as the horse and cart. Each object has its own set of forces, and you must keep them separate.

Think about the horse pushing its hooves into the ground. It is like when you try to walk on a slippery icy surface — you cannot push off properly, so you go nowhere. But on a normal road, the ground grips your foot and pushes you forward. That forward push from the ground on the horse is what actually drives the horse forward. Without that ground reaction force, the horse would just slide backward and the whole system would go nowhere, no matter how hard the horse pulled the cart.

Here is a fresh everyday example. Imagine a swimmer pushing off the wall of a pool. The swimmer pushes the wall backward, and the wall pushes the swimmer forward. If you only looked at the swimmer as your system, the only force you care about is the wall pushing the swimmer. The force the swimmer exerts on the wall belongs to the wall's story, not the swimmer's. The swimmer rockets forward because of the force on the swimmer, full stop. This is the same careful thinking the horse and cart problem demands.

Now think about what would happen if the road were perfectly frictionless under the horse's hooves, like a sheet of ice. The horse pulls the cart forward, the cart pulls the horse backward, and there is no ground force to help the horse. The horse would actually slide backward while the cart slides forward — which is exactly that funny image of the horse ending up sitting in the cart! The fact that this does not happen in real life is entirely because of friction between the horse's hooves and the road, which provides that crucial extra forward force on the horse.

5.7 INERTIA
A particle is accelerated (in an inertial frame) if
and only if a resultant force acts on it. Loosely
speaking, the particle does not change its state of rest
or of uniform motion along a straight line unless it is
forced to do this. This unwillingness of a particle to
change its state of rest or of uniform motion along a
straight line is called as inertia. We can understand
the property of inertia in more precise terms as follows.
If equal forces are applied on two particles, in general,
the acceleration of the particles will be different. The
property of a particle to allow a smaller acceleration
is called inertia. It is clear that larger the mass of the
particle, smaller will be the acceleration and hence
larger will be the inertia.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about one of the most fundamental ideas in all of physics — inertia. You already know from Newton's first law that an object sitting still tends to stay still, and an object moving in a straight line at constant speed tends to keep doing exactly that, unless some outside force steps in and changes things. Inertia is just the name we give to that tendency — that stubbornness, if you like, that every object has about changing its state of motion. Think of it as nature's way of saying, 'I was perfectly happy doing what I was doing, thank you very much.' Now here is where it gets really interesting. Imagine you push two different objects with exactly the same force — say, you give a gentle shove to a tennis ball and then the same shove to a bowling ball. The tennis ball shoots off quickly, but the bowling ball barely moves. Both felt the same force, yet their accelerations were very different. The bowling ball resisted the change in its motion far more than the tennis ball did. That resistance is inertia. The bowling ball has more inertia. And here is the key connection — the more mass an object has, the more inertia it has. Mass and inertia are two sides of the same coin. A large mass means a large resistance to acceleration. A small mass means the object is easier to get moving or to slow down. So when we say a particle has high inertia, we simply mean it takes a lot of force to change what it is doing. This is why a loaded truck is so much harder to stop than a bicycle moving at the same speed. The truck has far more mass, and therefore far more inertia. The mathematical heart of this idea comes straight from Newton's second law — force equals mass times acceleration, which means acceleration equals force divided by mass. So for the same force, a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration. Inertia is not a force itself — it is a property, a measure of how much an object fights back against being accelerated.
examples: Think about pushing a shopping cart that is completely empty versus one that is loaded up with heavy groceries. You use the same pushing force, but the full cart accelerates much more slowly. That is inertia at work. The loaded cart has more mass, so it resists the change in its motion more strongly. If you suddenly let go, the full cart also takes longer to slow down on its own. Its greater mass means greater inertia — a greater unwillingness to change whatever it is currently doing.

Here is a classic demonstration you might have seen. Place a coin on top of a piece of cardboard resting on a glass. Now flick the cardboard away sharply. The coin drops straight into the glass rather than flying off with the cardboard. Why? Because the coin has inertia — it was at rest, and the very brief flick of the cardboard did not apply enough force for long enough to drag the coin along with it. The coin simply stayed where it was, and gravity pulled it down into the glass. That is inertia in its purest form.

Imagine two balls — one made of solid iron and one made of hollow plastic — both the same size. If you apply the same kick to each, the plastic ball flies much farther. The iron ball has far more mass packed into the same space, so it has far more inertia. It resists the change in its motion much more strongly. This is exactly why the textbook tells us that the property of allowing a smaller acceleration when the same force is applied is what we call inertia — and larger mass always means larger inertia.

Think about a passenger in a car that suddenly brakes hard. The car slows down rapidly because the brakes apply a large force to it. But the passenger's body keeps wanting to move forward at the original speed — that is inertia. The passenger's body has mass, and that mass resists the sudden change in velocity. The seatbelt has to step in and apply a force to slow the passenger down along with the car. Without that force, the passenger would just keep going forward. This is a perfect everyday reminder that inertia is not laziness — it is a real, measurable property tied directly to mass.

events.text: Inertia is the resistance of an object to changes in its state of motion. More mass = more inertia.

Inertia keeps an object in its current state — at rest or in uniform motion — until a net force acts on it.

questions.q_text: A ball of mass two kilograms hangs motionless from a string attached to the ceiling. Using Newton's First Law and taking the gravitational acceleration as nine point eight metres per second squared, find the tension in the string.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify the state of motion. The ball is hanging at rest, which means its acceleration is exactly zero. Step 2 — Apply Newton's First Law. Because the acceleration is zero, the total force on the ball must be zero, meaning all forces acting on it must cancel out perfectly. Step 3 — List the forces. Two forces act on the ball: gravity pulling it downward, and the tension in the string pulling it upward. Step 4 — Calculate the gravitational force. Force of gravity equals mass times gravitational acceleration, which is two kilograms multiplied by nine point eight metres per second squared, giving nineteen point six newtons downward. Step 5 — Set the forces equal. For the total force to be zero, the upward tension must exactly equal the downward gravitational force. Therefore the tension in the string is nineteen point six newtons upward.

questions.answer: Step 1: Identify all forces acting on the box. There is a 50-newton push to the right and a 20-newton friction force to the left. Step 2: Calculate the net force by adding the forces, taking direction into account. Choosing right as positive: net force equals 50 newtons minus 20 newtons, which equals 30 newtons to the right. First, gravity pulls the lamp downward with a force equal to mass times gravitational acceleration, which is 2 times 10 equals 20 newtons downward. Second, the wire pulls the lamp upward with tension T. Step 3 — Draw the free body diagram: Represent the lamp as a dot. questions.q_text: A block of mass 3 kilograms hangs from a massless string attached to the ceiling. A second, identical 3-kilogram block hangs from the first block via another massless string. Taking g as 10 meters per second squared, find the tension in the upper string and the tension in the lower string. Then identify the Newton's Third Law partner of the tension force that the upper string exerts on the top block.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Analyze the lower block. The only forces on the lower block are its weight downward (3 kg times 10 = 30 newtons) and the tension in the lower string upward. Since the block is in equilibrium, the tension in the lower string equals 30 newtons.

Step 2 — Analyze the upper block. The forces on the upper block are: its own weight downward (30 newtons), the tension in the lower string pulling it downward (30 newtons, because the lower string pulls down on the upper block by Newton's Third Law), and the tension in the upper string pulling it upward. For equilibrium: upper tension = 30 + 30 = 60 newtons.

Step 3 — Identify the Third Law partner. The upper string pulls the top block upward with 60 newtons. By Newton's Third Law, the top block pulls the upper string downward with 60 newtons. These two forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects (one on the block, one on the string), making them a proper Third Law pair.

Final answers: Tension in lower string = 30 newtons. Tension in upper string = 60 newtons. The Third Law partner of the upward 60-newton force on the top block is the downward 60-newton force that the top block exerts on the upper string.

questions.q_text: A person of mass 60 kilograms stands on a scale inside an elevator that is accelerating upward at 3 metres per second squared. Using the pseudo force approach from inside the elevator frame, calculate the reading on the scale. Take gravitational acceleration as 10 metres per second squared.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the frame: We are working from inside the elevator, which is a noninertial frame accelerating upward at 3 metres per second squared.

Step 2 — List all forces on the person as seen from inside the elevator:
  • Weight acting downward: mass times gravitational acceleration = 60 times 10 = 600 newtons downward.
  • Normal force from the scale acting upward: this is what the scale reads, call it N.
  • Pseudo force: because the frame accelerates upward, the pseudo force points downward (opposite to the frame's acceleration), with magnitude = mass times frame acceleration = 60 times 3 = 180 newtons downward.

Step 3 — Apply Newton's second law from inside the elevator. From this frame, the person appears to be in equilibrium (not accelerating relative to the elevator), so the net force equals zero:
  N - 600 - 180 = 0

Step 4 — Solve for N:
  N = 600 + 180 = 780 newtons.

Step 5 — Interpret: The scale reads 780 newtons, which corresponds to an apparent weight of 780 divided by 10 = 78 kilograms-force. The person feels heavier than their actual 60 kg because the pseudo force adds to gravity inside the accelerating frame.
