Using the pseudo force approach, find the angle the string makes with the vertical. Take gravitational acceleration as 10 metres per second squared.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the frame: We work from inside the car, a noninertial frame accelerating forward at 5 metres per second squared.

Step 2 — Forces on the bob as seen from inside the car:
  • Weight: mass times 10, acting straight downward.
  • Tension T: acting along the string toward the ceiling attachment point.
  • Pseudo force: magnitude = mass times 5, acting backward (opposite to the car's forward acceleration).

Step 3 — The bob is in equilibrium inside the car, so horizontal and vertical force components must each sum to zero.

Step 4 — Vertical equilibrium:
  T times cosine(angle) = mass times 10

Step 5 — Horizontal equilibrium (taking backward as positive for the pseudo force):
  T times sine(angle) = mass times 5

Step 6 — Divide the horizontal equation by the vertical equation to eliminate T and mass:
  tangent(angle) = 5 divided by 10 = 0.5

Step 7 — Solve for the angle:
  angle = inverse tangent of 0.5 ≈ 26.6 degrees.

The string makes approximately 26.6 degrees with the vertical, tilting backward relative to the car's direction of motion.

questions.q_text: An observer on the ground and a passenger inside an accelerating train both watch a ball roll along the train floor. The ground observer correctly explains the ball's motion using only real forces and Newton's second law. The passenger inside the train also correctly explains the ball's motion using Newton's second law. Which of the following is true?
options: A. The passenger must introduce a pseudo force, while the ground observer needs no pseudo force
B. Both observers must introduce a pseudo force to get the correct answer
C. Neither observer needs a pseudo force because Newton's second law always works without one
D. The ground observer needs a pseudo force because the train's acceleration affects measurements from outside too

questions.q_text: A student says: 'The horse pulls the cart forward, but the cart pulls the horse backward with an equal force, so the net force is zero and nothing can move.' What is the fundamental error in this reasoning?
options: A. The two forces are not actually equal in size, so they do not cancel.
B. The two forces act on different objects, so they cannot be added together to find the net force on anything.
C. Newton's third law only applies when objects are not moving, so it should be ignored here.
D. The student forgot that the horse is heavier than the cart, which breaks the symmetry.

questions.q_text: Suppose the road under the horse's hooves is perfectly frictionless, like a sheet of ice. The horse still pulls the cart via the harness rope. What would actually happen?
options: A. The horse and cart move forward together because the horse's pull is stronger than the cart's pull.
B. Nothing moves at all because the two Newton's third law forces cancel out.
C. The horse slides backward and the cart slides forward, so they move in opposite directions.
D. Only the cart moves forward because the horse is the one doing the work.

questions.q_text: You want to calculate the acceleration of the cart alone. Which of the following correctly lists the forces you should include in your analysis?
options: A. The forward pull of the horse on the cart, and the backward pull of the cart on the horse.
B. The forward pull of the horse on the cart, and any friction from the road acting on the cart's wheels.
C. Only the backward pull of the cart on the horse, since that is the reaction force.
D. The forward pull of the horse on the cart, the backward pull of the cart on the horse, and friction from the road on the cart.

questions.q_text: Why does the horse accelerate forward even though the cart is pulling it backward?
options: A. Because the horse is more massive than the cart, so the same force produces less acceleration on the horse.
B. Because the horse ignores the backward pull from the cart by using its muscles.
C. Because the ground pushes the horse forward via friction, and if that forward push is larger than the cart's backward pull, the horse has a net forward force.
D. Because Newton's third law does not apply to living animals, only to inanimate objects.

questions.q_text: A horse of mass 500 kg is pulling a cart of mass 300 kg along a flat road. The ground pushes the horse forward with a friction force of 1200 newtons. The road exerts a backward friction force of 240 newtons on the cart's wheels. The horse and cart move together as one unit. Find: (1) the acceleration of the whole system, and (2) the tension in the harness rope connecting the horse to the cart.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify the system and the external forces. When we treat the horse and cart together as one combined system, the internal forces (the rope tension pulling horse backward and cart forward) cancel out. The only external horizontal forces are the ground pushing the horse forward with 1200 newtons, and friction pushing the cart backward with 240 newtons. Step 2 — Find the net force on the combined system. Net force equals 1200 minus 240, which equals 960 newtons forward. Step 3 — Find the total mass. Total mass equals 500 plus 300, which equals 800 kilograms. Step 4 — Apply net force equals mass times acceleration. Acceleration equals 960 divided by 800, which equals 1.2 metres per second squared forward. Both the horse and cart share this same acceleration since they move as one unit. Step 5 — Find the rope tension by analysing the cart alone. The forces on the cart are: the rope pulling it forward with tension T, and road friction pushing it backward with 240 newtons. Applying net force equals mass times acceleration for the cart: T minus 240 equals 300 times 1.2, so T minus 240 equals 360, so T equals 600 newtons. Step 6 — Verify using the horse alone. Forces on the horse: ground friction forward 1200 newtons, rope pulling backward 600 newtons. Net force equals 1200 minus 600 equals 600 newtons. Acceleration equals 600 divided by 500 equals 1.2 metres per second squared. This matches, confirming the answer. Final answers: acceleration equals 1.2 metres per second squared, and rope tension equals 600 newtons.

questions.q_text: A student says, 'Inertia is the force that keeps a moving object going.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: A. Inertia only applies to objects that are stationary, not moving ones.
B. Inertia is not a force at all — it is a property of matter that describes resistance to changes in motion.
C. The statement is correct; inertia is indeed a type of force.
D. Inertia only exists when friction is absent.

questions.q_text: You apply exactly the same force to a 2 kg block and a 10 kg block. Which of the following correctly describes what happens, and why?
options: A. Both blocks accelerate at the same rate because the force is identical.
B. The 10 kg block accelerates faster because larger objects respond better to force.
C. The 2 kg block accelerates five times faster than the 10 kg block because it has less mass and therefore less inertia.
D. The 10 kg block accelerates faster because it has more inertia to overcome the friction.

questions.q_text: In the coin-and-cardboard demonstration, the cardboard is flicked away quickly and the coin drops into the glass below. If you replaced the coin with a much heavier metal disc of the same size, what would you expect to happen, and why?
options: A. The heavier disc would fly off with the cardboard more easily because it has more momentum.
B. The heavier disc would still drop into the glass — in fact its greater mass means even more inertia, so it resists being dragged along even more strongly.
C. The heavier disc would fly off because the cardboard would exert a larger force on it.
D. The result would be completely unpredictable because weight changes the friction between the disc and cardboard.

questions.q_text: A bicycle and its rider together have a mass of 80 kg and are moving at 10 metres per second. A truck has a mass of 8000 kg and is also moving at 10 metres per second. Both need to stop completely. Using the concept of inertia and Newton's second law, explain why the truck is so much harder to stop, and calculate how many times more force the truck requires to stop in the same distance and time as the bicycle.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Understand what stopping means in terms of physics. To stop, both the bicycle and the truck must go from 10 metres per second to zero. Since they are travelling at the same speed and must stop over the same time, they need the same change in velocity. By Newton's second law, force equals mass times acceleration. The acceleration needed is the same for both (same speed change, same time), so the only difference in the force required comes from the difference in mass.

Step 2 — Compare the masses. The truck's mass is 8000 kg and the bicycle's mass is 80 kg. The ratio of their masses is 8000 divided by 80, which equals 100.

Step 3 — Apply Newton's second law. Since force equals mass times acceleration, and the required acceleration is identical for both, the force needed is directly proportional to mass. The truck therefore requires 100 times more force to stop in the same time over the same distance.

Step 4 — Connect to inertia. The truck has 100 times more mass than the bicycle. Because inertia is directly tied to mass, the truck has 100 times more inertia — meaning it resists the change in its motion 100 times more strongly. This is precisely why a loaded truck needs powerful brakes and a much longer stopping distance compared to a bicycle: its enormous inertia fights against any attempt to alter its state of motion.

questions.q_text: A heavier passenger and a lighter passenger are sitting in the same car travelling at the same speed. The car brakes suddenly. Ignoring all other factors, which passenger's seatbelt must exert more force to stop them, and what principle explains this?
options: A. Both seatbelts exert the same force because the car decelerates at the same rate for everyone inside.
B. The lighter passenger's seatbelt exerts more force because lighter people are more sensitive to sudden changes.

C. The heavier passenger's seatbelt must exert more force, because the heavier passenger has greater mass and therefore greater inertia — more resistance to the change in motion — requiring a larger force to produce the same deceleration.
D. Neither seatbelt exerts any force; they only prevent the passenger from falling out of the seat.
